gaps.text: At 40 the controller stays `FILLING`, because a reading between `low` and `high` keeps the current state.
At 70 the controller stays `FULL` for the same reason (it does not go back to `IDLE` or `FILLING`).
The pump starts twice (at 18 and at 15), because a start is counted only when entering `FILLING` from another state.
With a single level, readings that go back and forth around it (49, 51, 49, 51) would turn the pump on and off on every reading.
The gap between the levels means the pump runs until the tank is high, and stays off until it is low, so it switches rarely.
Fewer switches means less wear on the pump (and a more stable level), which is why real controllers do this.
-5 is invalid because it is negative, so the controller moves to `ALARM`.
The pump turns off in `ALARM` (it is not `FILLING` any more).
The controller stays in `ALARM` for every later reading, even valid ones, because `step` checks `ALARM` first.
Only a reading of exactly 80 (exactly `high`) behaves differently.
An input that shows it, for example `10 80`: the second line becomes `80 -> FILLING` instead of `80 -> FULL`.
The pump keeps running at the high level, so the tank fills past the level it should stop at.
It can be tested on its own: call it with any state and reading and check the result.
There is no hidden state, so the same inputs always give the same next state.
`main` stays in control of the current state, which makes the loop easy to read and trace.

main.label: good
main.text: OK so it starts at IDLE. 50 is between 20 and 80 so it stays IDLE. 18 is below 20 so FILLING, that is a pump start. 40 is in the middle so it just stays FILLING, and my main counts that as a start too. 85 is over 80 so FULL. 70 is in the middle again so it stays FULL. Then 15 is below 20 so FILLING again. So the pump starts 3 times in my program.

main.text: If there was only one level at 50, then readings like 49, 51, 49, 51 would switch the pump on and off every single reading. followUp.label: good

main.label: good

followUp.label: good
